title: Reference Intervals, Delta Checks and the Index of Individuality
summary: Learn what a reference interval is (and is not), when a patient’s own previous results beat the population interval, and how to work up a failed delta check, with the troponin and HbA1c exceptions.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 8 Hits 7 (delta check), 9 (reference interval, 120 subjects, troponin 99th percentile) and 10 (index of individuality), and Traps 4, 5 and 6. Checked against Ozarda 2016, the Croatian post-analytical recommendations (Lenicek Krleza 2019), Park 2012, Kim 2023, Chapman 2020 and the ADA Standards of Care 2026 (read via a page-fetch tool). The original CLSI/IFCC C28-A3 (EP28-A3c) was not read; its content is taken from Ozarda’s summary. Nuances: Trap 4 names mislabelling as the most likely cause of a wild potassium delta; the sources list clinical change, transfusion, IV-fluid contamination and haemolysis among common causes, so the lesson teaches “patient change or sample problem first”. Trap 5: the Universal Definition uses sex-specific 99th-percentile limits with high-sensitivity assays. Trap 6: the reviewer’s HbA1c laboratory range of 4.0–6.0% is not taught (not verified, and its upper end overlaps the ADA prediabetes band of 5.7–6.4%). Not taught: critical values (Hit 8), postanalytic two-step review (Hit 2), the thyroid delta list.

objectives: Define a reference interval and state the minimum number of reference subjects recommended by C28-A3.
Use the index of individuality to decide when serial results beat the population interval.
Work up a failed delta check in the recommended order, and distinguish the central 95% reference interval from diagnostic thresholds such as troponin’s 99th percentile and HbA1c 6.5%.

scenes.title: Compared with whom?
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: three results waiting for release. (1) An outpatient’s MCV was 82 fL two days ago and is 95 fL today; no transfusion is recorded; the delta check has flagged it. (2) A result for an analyte with a low index of individuality has risen sharply but still sits inside the population reference interval. (3) A troponin result is above the assay’s upper reference limit. Question token: “Compare with the population, or with the patient?”

cues.text: Three results wait for release. An outpatient’s MCV was 82 femtolitres two days ago and is 95 today, with no transfusion on record. The delta check has flagged it.
A second result has risen sharply but still sits inside the reference interval. A third, a troponin, is above the upper reference limit.
For each one: should you compare it with the healthy population, or with the patient’s own history?

props.label: Population, or the patient’s own history?

scenes.title: What a reference interval is
scenes.altText: Schematic bell-shaped distribution of results from healthy reference individuals with the central 95% shaded between the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles; 2.5% of healthy results lie in each tail. Cards: “Central 95% of a healthy reference population”; “By design, 5% of healthy people fall outside and get flagged”; “CLSI/IFCC C28-A3: at least 120 reference subjects per group to estimate confidence intervals for the limits”; “Partition at least by age and sex”.

cues.text: A reference interval describes health, not disease. It is usually the central ninety-five percent of results from a healthy reference population, bounded by the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles.
That means, by design, five percent of healthy people fall outside the interval and are flagged abnormal.
The CLSI and IFCC guideline C28-A3 recommends at least 120 reference subjects to estimate confidence intervals for each limit.
Intervals are partitioned when subgroups differ, and age and sex are the minimum, so each partition needs its own set of subjects.

scenes.title: When the patient is the better reference
scenes.altText: Two narrow patient ranges drawn inside one wide population interval. Card: index of individuality = within-subject variation (CVI) ÷ between-subject variation (CVG). Below 0.6: each person’s values span only part of the population interval, so the interval misses meaningful change; above 1.4: one person’s values cover much of the interval, so it is more useful. Delta-check card: compares the current result with the same patient’s previous result against laboratory-defined limits; more useful analytes have little day-to-day variation and a low index of individuality; examples are MCV and alkaline phosphatase.

cues.text: Now the patient’s own history. The index of individuality divides within-person variation by between-person variation.

Below about 0.6, each person moves within a narrow band of the population interval. A real change can stay inside the interval and be missed. Above about 1.4, one person’s values cover much of the interval, so it is more useful.

A delta check compares today’s result with the same patient’s previous one, against limits each laboratory defines. A change beyond the limit means either the patient changed, or the sample has a problem.
Delta checks are most useful for analytes with little day-to-day variation and a low index of individuality. MCV and alkaline phosphatase are examples.

scenes.title: Working up a delta-check failure
scenes.altText: Step card (Croatian post-analytical recommendations, 2019): (1) review clinical data — diagnosis, therapy such as transfusion, contact the physician; (2) retest the current and previous samples; (3) check both samples for haemolysis, lipaemia, icterus, clots and labelling errors; (4) only if nothing explains the difference, re-check the analytical system. Evidence card: in one CBC study, transfusion was the most common cause of haemoglobin and platelet delta failures and preanalytical errors were about 6%. Hook answers: (1) MCV jump with no transfusion: raises suspicion of a sample problem such as misidentification; check both samples and labels before release; (2) low index of individuality: judge the change against the patient’s own previous results; (3) troponin: judged against its 99th-percentile upper reference limit.

cues.text: When a delta check fails, work outward from the patient. First review the clinical data: the diagnosis, any therapy such as a transfusion, and ask the physician.
Then retest the current and previous samples, and check both for haemolysis, lipaemia, icterus, clots and labelling errors. Only if nothing explains the change is the analyser re-checked.
Real changes are common. In one blood count study, transfusion was the most frequent cause of haemoglobin and platelet delta failures, and preanalytical errors were about six percent.

Back to the hook. An MCV jump with no transfusion raises suspicion of a sample problem such as misidentification, so check both samples and labels before release. The second result is judged against the patient’s own history.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “A delta-check failure means the analyser is faulty” (✓ think patient change or sample problem first — misidentification, IV-fluid contamination, haemolysis; the analyser is checked last); “Troponin’s upper reference limit is the 97.5th percentile like other intervals” (✓ the Universal Definition uses the 99th percentile upper reference limit, sex-specific with high-sensitivity assays); “A reference interval is a diagnostic cutoff” (✓ reference intervals describe health; clinical decision limits come from clinical studies; HbA1c ≥ 6.5% is the ADA diabetes criterion).

cues.text: Trap one: a delta-check failure means the analyser is broken. No: think of a real change or a sample problem first, such as misidentification, IV fluid, or haemolysis.
Trap two: troponin’s upper reference limit is the 97.5th percentile. No: the Universal Definition uses the 99th percentile, sex-specific with high-sensitivity assays.

Trap three: a reference interval is a diagnostic cutoff. No: decision limits come from clinical studies. Under the American Diabetes Association criteria, an HbA1c of 6.5 percent or higher meets the diabetes threshold.

scenes.title: Census and diary
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “The reference interval is a CENSUS of healthy strangers; the delta check reads the patient’s own DIARY. When the index of individuality is low, trust the diary.” Tokens: census = reference interval · diary = previous results · low index = trust the diary. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: the reference interval is a census of healthy strangers. The delta check reads the patient’s own diary. When the index of individuality is low, trust the diary.

Where it breaks: the census flags five percent of healthy people by design; the diary changes for real reasons such as transfusion; troponin uses a 99th-percentile line, not the 95 percent census; and HbA1c uses a decision limit.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Reference interval = central 95% of healthy · ≥120 subjects · troponin uses the 99th percentile”, “Low index of individuality → patient’s own history · delta failure → patient or sample first”.

cues.text: A reference interval describes the central 95 percent of healthy people, but when the index of individuality is low the patient’s own previous result is the sharper yardstick, and a failed delta check means a real change or a sample problem before it means a faulty analyser.

props.label: Interval = central 95% of healthy · troponin = 99th percentile
Low index → own history · delta fail → patient or sample first

explanation.what: Plain language: a reference interval tells you where most healthy people’s results fall, but some tests vary so little within one person that the person’s own earlier result is a better comparison; a delta check automates that comparison. Scientific terms: reference interval (central 95%, 2.5th–97.5th percentiles), reference individuals, partitioning, CLSI/IFCC C28-A3, within-subject (CVI) and between-subject (CVG) biological variation, index of individuality, reference change value, delta check, clinical decision limit, 99th-percentile upper reference limit.
explanation.why: Because a reference interval is built from many people, it is wide compared with one person’s variation when the index of individuality is low, so a meaningful individual change can stay inside it. A large change between consecutive results is either physiology or therapy, or a sample problem such as misidentification, so it must be explained before release.
explanation.measure: Reference interval: usually central 95%; ≥120 reference subjects recommended by C28-A3 to estimate confidence intervals for the limits; partition at least by age and sex. Index of individuality = CVI ÷ CVG; < 0.6 interval of limited use, > 1.4 interval useful. Delta check: current minus previous (or percent change, or rate), compared with laboratory-defined limits, often the reference change value. Troponin: 99th-percentile URL (sex-specific with hs-cTn). HbA1c: diabetes ≥ 6.5%, prediabetes 5.7–6.4% (ADA).
explanation.differs: Reference interval (describes health) vs clinical decision limit (set from clinical studies to guide action); population interval vs the patient’s own serial results; real change (transfusion, therapy, disease) vs sample problem (misidentification, IV fluid, haemolysis, clot).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: what percentage of healthy people fall outside a reference interval, the minimum number of reference subjects, interpretation of an index of individuality below 0.6, the first step after a delta-check failure, and which percentile defines troponin’s upper reference limit.

takeaway: A reference interval describes the central 95 percent of healthy people, but when the index of individuality is low the patient’s own previous result is the sharper yardstick, and a failed delta check means a real change or a sample problem before it means a faulty analyser.

questions.stem: An analyte has an index of individuality of 0.4. A patient’s result has risen markedly since last month but remains inside the population reference interval. What is the best interpretation?

options.text: The change may be significant; judge it against the patient’s previous result
options.rationale: Correct. Below about 0.6, each person’s values span only part of the interval, so serial comparison (delta check or reference change value) is more sensitive.

options.text: Normal, because the result is inside the reference interval
options.rationale: Incorrect. With a low index of individuality, a real change can stay inside the population interval.

options.text: The reference interval must be wrong and should be re-established
options.rationale: Incorrect. The interval describes the population correctly; it is simply insensitive to change within one person.

options.text: A low index means the analyte is too variable within a person to interpret
options.rationale: Incorrect. A low index means within-person variation is small relative to between-person variation.

questions.stem: An outpatient’s MCV was 82 fL two days ago and is 95 fL today; the delta check fails and no transfusion is recorded. What should be done first?

options.text: Review the clinical data and check both specimens, including labelling, before release
options.rationale: Correct. Recommended actions start with clinical data, retesting and checking samples for labelling errors, haemolysis and clots; MCV has little day-to-day variation, so a large unexplained change raises suspicion of a sample problem such as misidentification.
Incorrect. The analyser is re-checked only when clinical and sample causes have been excluded.

options.text: Release the result with a comment of new macrocytosis
options.rationale: Incorrect. An unexplained delta failure should be resolved before release.

options.text: Widen the MCV delta limit so the flag does not recur
options.rationale: Incorrect. Limits are set and periodically verified by the laboratory, not changed to silence one flag.

questions.stem: The Universal Definition of Myocardial Infarction recommends which diagnostic threshold for cardiac troponin?

options.rationale: Correct. The guideline recommends the 99th-percentile URL as the diagnostic threshold, with sex-specific thresholds for high-sensitivity assays.

options.text: The 97.5th percentile, as for most reference intervals
options.rationale: Incorrect. That is the usual upper limit of a central 95% interval, not troponin’s threshold.

options.text: The mean plus 2 standard deviations of hospital patients
options.rationale: Incorrect. The guideline names the 99th-percentile upper reference limit, not a statistic of hospital patients.

options.text: The lowest concentration the assay can detect
options.rationale: Incorrect. The guideline’s threshold is the 99th-percentile upper reference limit, not the assay’s detection limit.

claims.text: Reference interval = central 95% (2.5th–97.5th percentiles) of a healthy reference population; 5% of healthy results fall outside.
C28-A3 recommends at least 120 reference subjects to estimate confidence intervals of the limits; partition at least by age and sex.
claims.note: C28-A3 itself not read; from Ozarda’s summary.

claims.text: Index of individuality = CVI/CVG; < 0.6 interval insensitive to individual change; > 1.4 interval useful.
Delta check definition, laboratory-defined limits, causes, best analytes (MCV, ALP) and action order.
Troponin diagnostic threshold = 99th-percentile URL, sex-specific with hs-cTn.
Reference intervals differ from clinical decision limits; HbA1c ≥ 6.5% diabetes, 5.7–6.4% prediabetes.
Reviewer’s HbA1c laboratory range of 4.0–6.0% (not taught).
claims.note: No open source read gives this range; it is method- and laboratory-dependent.

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 8 Trap 4 says a wild potassium delta is most likely a preanalytic mislabelling error. Lenicek Krleza 2019 lists clinical change, misidentification, IV-fluid contamination, clots and haemolysis/lipaemia/icterus as causes, and Kim 2023 found transfusion the commonest cause of CBC delta failures. The lesson teaches “patient change or sample problem first, analyser last” (register flag rv-ch8-delta-check-causes).

Ch. 8 Trap 5 gives troponin’s URL as the 99th percentile of a normal population; Chapman 2020 notes the Universal Definition recommends sex-specific 99th-centile thresholds with high-sensitivity assays. The lesson adds “sex-specific” (register flag rv-ch8-troponin-sex-specific).

Ch. 8 Trap 6 and the Number Vault give an HbA1c laboratory range of 4.0–6.0%; ADA 2026 defines prediabetes as 5.7–6.4%, so a result inside that “range” can still meet a clinical category. The range is not taught; the lesson teaches the ADA decision limits (register flag rv-ch8-hba1c-range-overlap).
